title: What is a black hole?
subject: Astronomy
attribution: “What is a black hole? Astro-Investigates Ep. 1” by NASA/JPL-Caltech (NASA Scientific Visualization Studio, SVS 14621). Public domain (NASA). From the 1080p master on the NASA SVS page; transcoded to 1080p H.264/AAC.

recaps.text: Black holes are places where gravity is so intense that not even light can escape. They are extremely dense, real objects, and not really “holes”.
Stellar-mass black holes form when massive stars collapse; supermassive ones sit at the centres of galaxies. Black holes don’t “suck”: you can orbit one like any other massive object.
Matter falling in spins into a hot, bright accretion disk. The 2019 black-hole image showed this glowing “donut” around a dark centre.
Close to a black hole, time appears to slow and tidal forces can stretch a star apart (a tidal disruption event). At the very centre, general relativity breaks down.
Astronomers find black holes from their X-ray, optical, ultraviolet and infrared light, and from gravitational waves when two black holes merge.
Open questions: how supermassive black holes grew so large and what lies beyond the event horizon. Cygnus X-1, found in 1964 from its X-rays, became the earliest confirmed black hole.

recallQuestions.question: Why is a black hole called “black”?
choices: Not even light can escape it
It is made of dark matter

recallQuestions.question: What happens to an object orbiting a black hole at a safe distance?
choices: It can keep orbiting, as around any massive object
It speeds up until it escapes

recallQuestions.question: What forms as matter spirals toward a black hole?
Which black hole was confirmed earliest?

title: Travel deep inside a leaf
subject: Biology
source: California Academy of Sciences (via Wikimedia Commons)
attribution: “Travel Deep Inside a Leaf – Annotated Version” by California Academy of Sciences, licensed CC BY 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/). Via Wikimedia Commons; transcoded from the original 720p upload to H.264/AAC.

recaps.text: We zoom from a redwood tree into a single leaf and toward a stoma, a tiny pore in the leaf surface, going from the centimetre to the millimetre scale.
Inside the leaf are palisade cells, where photosynthesis takes place. They are translucent so sunlight can get in.
Inside one cell: the Golgi apparatus, endoplasmic reticulum studded with ribosomes, the nucleus, mitochondria and the cytoskeleton that supports the cell.
Chloroplasts contain flat membranes called thylakoids, where the light-dependent reactions make ATP. Photosystems in the membrane absorb light energy.
ATP synthase, a rotating enzyme, assembles ATP as protons cross the membrane. Energised electrons pass between photosystems like a bucket brigade, and ATP stores the energy that powers life.

recallQuestions.question: In which leaf cells does photosynthesis mainly take place?
Where in the chloroplast do the light-dependent reactions happen?
What does the enzyme ATP synthase do?

title: How a laser works
subject: Engineering
attribution: “How a Laser Works” (EngineerGuy Series #4) by Bill Hammack, engineerguy, licensed CC BY 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/). Via Wikimedia Commons; transcoded to 1080p H.264/AAC.

recaps.text: Laser light has three special properties: a nearly single wavelength, a narrow beam and high intensity. Eye surgeons use all three to weld a detached retina back into place, treating spots as small as 30 microns.
A glow-in-the-dark toy shows the basic idea: light lifts electrons to higher energy levels, and when they fall back to the ground state the lost energy comes out as light.
In 1960 Ted Maiman built the first laser from a ruby cylinder surrounded by a xenon flash lamp. With a weak lamp, excited electrons fall back on their own and give off incoherent light.

Repeated powerful flashes (pumping) create a population inversion: more electrons in the excited level than in the ground state. One emitted photon then triggers an avalanche of identical photons (stimulated emission), giving coherent light.

Maiman silvered the ends of the rod, parallel to within 200 nanometres. In this resonant cavity, off-axis rays escape out of the sides and a standing wave leaves a nearly single wavelength. A partly silvered mirror lets the beam out.
Today lasers are cheap: a laser pointer uses a semiconductor diode. Many improvements have come since 1960, but the essential principles are the same.

recallQuestions.question: Why do eye surgeons use green laser light to repair a detached retina?
choices: It passes through the lens without being strongly absorbed, then the retina absorbs it
It is the only colour a laser can make
It makes the retina glow in the dark

recallQuestions.question: What material was the first laser, built in 1960, based on?
What does stimulated emission produce?
choices: Light of every colour at random
Coherent light, with the crests and troughs of the waves lined up

recallQuestions.question: What do the two parallel mirrored ends of the ruby rod do?
choices: Form a resonant cavity that narrows the beam and its wavelength
